svg.aria-label: Diagram: the dual-write problem and how an outbox built on DynamoDB addresses it, including where the guarantee stops. On the left, the broken shape: an application performs two writes, one to a database and one to a message broker, with no transaction spanning them, so a crash between the two leaves the state change without its event, or the event without its state change, and neither ordering is safe. In the middle, the fix: a single TransactWriteItems call writes the entity and an outbox record together as one all-or-nothing operation of up to 100 actions, limited to one AWS account and one Region with an aggregate size of four megabytes, and costing double because DynamoDB writes every item twice, once to prepare and once to commit. On the right, the relay: DynamoDB Streams derives change records from that same committed write, each stream record appears exactly once in the stream, ordering is guaranteed per individual item rather than across a partition, and records are retained for 24 hours. A panel across the bottom records where atomicity stops: AWS states that stream records from the same transaction might appear at different times and could be interleaved with records from other transactions, and that stream consumers should not assume transaction atomicity or ordering guarantees, so a consumer seeing the outbox record before the entity is supported behaviour. A second panel records that a write which does not change any data produces no stream record at all, so an idempotent no-op retry emits nothing unless each outbox record carries a unique key.
svg.title: The transaction guarantees the write, not the events derived from it
svg.text: One transaction removes the dual write. It does not reach the consumer.
Each box below carries a guarantee. The failures live in the gaps between them.
a retry needs a live process.
Where the atomicity stops — stated by AWS, not inferred
“Stream records from the same transaction might appear at different times and could be interleaved with records from other transactions.”
“Stream consumers shouldn’t assume transaction atomicity or ordering guarantees.”
A consumer that sees the outbox record before the entity is seeing supported behaviour, not a bug.
And a write that changes nothing is silent
“If you perform a PutItem or UpdateItem operation that does not change any data in an item, DynamoDB Streams does not write a stream record.”
Give every outbox record a unique key, or the idempotent retry you built emits nothing at all.
The transaction does the one job it can: making sure the event exists. Everything after it has to be true on its own.
